```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(shapviz)

# Loads tidymodels, the shared constants and the model-card helpers
# (section 12).
source("modeling_functions.R")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

model_colour     <- "#4C6EF5"
benchmark_colour <- "#868E96"

pct   <- \(x, accuracy = 0.1) percent(x, accuracy = accuracy)
money <- \(x) paste0(comma(x / 1e6), "M")
```

```{r load}
# Every fit below is loaded from the modeling notebook's caches; nothing is
# refit. The cache lines are captured and checked here (and listed in the
# appendix) rather than printed into the card.
cache_log <- capture.output({
  prepared <- load_prepared()
  train    <- prepared$train
  test     <- prepared$test

  cv_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)

  compare_data  <- stratified_sample(train, prop = COMPARE_PROP)
  compare_folds <- make_cv_folds(compare_data)
  tune_data     <- stratified_sample(train, n = TUNE_N)
  tune_folds    <- make_cv_folds(tune_data)

  xgb_tune_wf <- workflow(build_recipe(tune_data), xgb_tune_spec())
  xgb_grid    <- random_tune_grid(xgb_tune_wf, tune_data, size = 20)
  xgb_tuning  <- tune_grid_cached("xgb_tuning", xgb_tune_wf, tune_folds,
                                  xgb_grid, cv_metrics)

  xgb_rescored <- rescore_top(xgb_tuning, xgb_tune_wf, compare_folds, cv_metrics, n = 3)
  best_config  <- map(xgb_rescored, \(f) collect_metrics(f$result)) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = ".config") |>
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
    slice_max(mean, n = 1) |>
    pull(.config)
  best_params <- show_best(xgb_tuning$result, metric = "roc_auc", n = 3) |>
    filter(.config == best_config) |>
    select(mtry:sample_size)

  trees_sweep <- sweep_trees(extract_preprocessor(xgb_tune_wf), best_params,
                             trees = c(500, 1000, 1500, 2000),
                             folds = compare_folds, metrics = cv_metrics)
  best_trees  <- pick_trees(trees_sweep)

  final_exclude <- "CODE_GENDER"

  cv_nogender <- fit_resamples_cached("xgb_tuned_nogender",
    finalize_workflow(
      workflow(build_recipe(compare_data, exclude = final_exclude),
               xgb_tune_spec(trees = best_trees)),
      best_params),
    compare_folds, cv_metrics)

  # Pre-deployment check: the final configuration without marital status too.
  cv_nofamily <- fit_resamples_cached("xgb_tuned_nogender_nofamily",
    finalize_workflow(
      workflow(build_recipe(compare_data, exclude = c(final_exclude, "NAME_FAMILY_STATUS")),
               xgb_tune_spec(trees = best_trees)),
      best_params),
    compare_folds, cv_metrics)

  final_wf <- finalize_workflow(
    workflow(build_recipe(train, exclude = final_exclude),
             xgb_tune_spec(trees = best_trees)),
    best_params)

  final     <- fit_final_cached("xgb_tuned_final_nogender", final_wf, train)
  final_fit <- final$result

  full_folds <- make_cv_folds(train)
  oof <- oof_predictions_cached("xgb_final_oof", final_wf, full_folds, cv_metrics)
})

stopifnot(length(cache_log) > 0,
          all(str_starts(cache_log, "Loaded cached result")))

# The rebuilt configuration must match the saved final model exactly.
saved_args <- map(extract_spec_parsnip(final_fit)$args, rlang::eval_tidy)
stopifnot(all(map_lgl(names(best_params), \(p)
                as.numeric(best_params[[p]]) == as.numeric(saved_args[[p]]))),
          best_trees == as.numeric(saved_args$trees))
```

```{r scored}
# Raw AMT_CREDIT (the prepared data caps it at the 99th percentile) and raw
# CODE_GENDER (the prepared data imputes its 4 XNA rows to the mode, F).
prep_env  <- new.env()
source("data_preparation.R", local = prep_env)
raw_train <- prep_env$read_application("data/application_train.csv")
stopifnot(identical(raw_train$SK_ID_CURR, train$SK_ID_CURR))

scored <- oof$result$predictions |>
  arrange(.row) |>
  transmute(fold        = id,
            SK_ID_CURR  = train$SK_ID_CURR[.row],
            TARGET,
            default     = TARGET == "1",
            model_risk  = .pred_1,
            credit      = raw_train$AMT_CREDIT[.row],
            ext_source  = train$EXT_SOURCE_MEAN[.row],
            gender      = raw_train$CODE_GENDER[.row],
            education   = train$NAME_EDUCATION_TYPE[.row],
            age_band    = train$AGE_BAND[.row])

n_applicants <- nrow(scored)
per_100k     <- 1e5 / n_applicants

stopifnot(n_applicants == 307511,
          n_distinct(scored$SK_ID_CURR) == n_applicants,
          identical(scored$TARGET, train$TARGET),
          !anyNA(scored$credit))
```

```{r threshold-compute}
# Computed here because the performance section reports results at the
# chosen threshold.
cutoffs  <- seq(0.02, 0.40, by = 0.005)
sweep    <- cutoff_sweep(scored$model_risk, scored$default, scored$credit, cutoffs)
everyone <- cutoff_sweep(scored$model_risk, scored$default, scored$credit, cutoffs = 1)
stopifnot(everyone$approval_rate == 1)

scenarios <- tribble(
  ~scenario,          ~margin, ~lgd,
  "Base",             0.15,    0.90,
  "Lenient recovery", 0.15,    0.45,
  "Thin margin",      0.05,    0.90,
  "High margin",      0.20,    0.90
) |>
  mutate(scenario   = fct_inorder(scenario),
         break_even = break_even_cutoff(margin, lgd))

scenario_curves <- scenarios |>
  pmap(\(scenario, margin, lgd, break_even)
    add_profit(sweep, margin, lgd) |> mutate(scenario = scenario)) |>
  list_rbind()

optima <- scenario_curves |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  slice_max(profit, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(scenarios, by = "scenario") |>
  mutate(everyone_profit = map2_dbl(margin, lgd, \(m, l) add_profit(everyone, m, l)$profit),
         vs_everyone     = profit - everyone_profit)

# An optimum on the edge of the sweep would mean the range is too narrow.
stopifnot(all(optima$cutoff > min(cutoffs) & optima$cutoff < max(cutoffs)))

base <- optima |> filter(scenario == "Base")
chosen_cutoff <- round(base$cutoff / 0.005) * 0.005

# How flat the base-case curve is near its peak.
near_peak <- scenario_curves |>
  filter(scenario == "Base", profit >= 0.999 * base$profit) |>
  pull(cutoff) |>
  range()

at_chosen <- threshold_metrics(scored$model_risk, scored$default, chosen_cutoff)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(select(at_chosen$confusion, -outcome)), 1e5)))
```

```{r explain-compute}
# SHAP values for 1,000 unseen test applicants.
shap_sample <- withr::with_seed(MODEL_SEED, slice_sample(test, n = 1000))
shap_risk   <- predict(final_fit, shap_sample, type = "prob")$.pred_1

# xgb_contributions() checks that baseline plus contributions reproduces the
# workflow's predicted probability for every row before returning.
contrib <- xgb_contributions(final_fit, shap_sample)
factor_cols <- names(select(train, where(is.factor), -TARGET))

baseline_log_odds <- contrib |> filter(feature == "BIAS") |> pull(contribution) |> unique()

shap_long <- contrib |>
  filter(feature != "BIAS") |>
  mutate(factor = feature_group(feature, factor_cols))

grouped <- shap_long |>
  group_by(.row, factor) |>
  summarise(contribution = sum(contribution), .groups = "drop")

stopifnot(nrow(shap_sample) == 1000,
          n_distinct(shap_sample$SK_ID_CURR) == 1000,
          length(baseline_log_odds) == 1,
          # Grouping only regroups: each row's contributions still sum to its log-odds.
          isTRUE(all.equal(
            baseline_log_odds + as.numeric(tapply(grouped$contribution, grouped$.row, sum)),
            qlogis(shap_risk), tolerance = 1e-5)))

importance <- grouped |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  summarise(mean_abs = mean(abs(contribution)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = mean_abs / sum(mean_abs)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_abs))

shap_wide <- contrib |>
  filter(feature != "BIAS") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = feature, values_from = contribution) |>
  arrange(.row)

feature_values <- bake(extract_recipe(final_fit), shap_sample, all_predictors()) |>
  select(all_of(setdiff(names(shap_wide), ".row"))) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

```{r adverse-compute}
declined_rows <- which(shap_risk > chosen_cutoff)

# Each declined applicant's top three risk-increasing factors.
declined_top3 <- grouped |>
  filter(.row %in% declined_rows, contribution > 0) |>
  group_by(.row) |>
  slice_max(contribution, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(select(factor_map, factor, type), by = "factor")

top_factors <- importance |> slice_head(n = 10)
stopifnot(n_distinct(declined_top3$.row) == length(declined_rows),
          all(top_factors$factor %in% factor_map$factor),
          all(declined_top3$factor %in% factor_map$factor))

declined_counts <- declined_top3 |> count(factor, name = "in_top3")

flagged_types <- c("Sensitive", "Hard to explain")

coverage <- declined_top3 |>
  group_by(.row) |>
  summarise(any_flagged   = any(type %in% flagged_types),
            first_flagged = type[rank == 1] %in% flagged_types,
            any_sensitive = any(type == "Sensitive"),
            first_opaque  = type[rank == 1] == "Opaque score",
            any_term      = any(factor == "Payment relative to loan (implied term)"),
            .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(nrow(coverage) == length(declined_rows))
```

```{r fairness}
fairness_table <- function(outcomes, group_label) {
  outcomes |>
    transmute(group = as.character(group),
              applicants = comma(applicants),
              actual_default_rate = pct(actual_default_rate, 0.01),
              approval_rate = pct(approval_rate, 0.1),
              approved_default_rate = pct(approved_default_rate, 0.01),
              impact_ratio = number(impact_ratio, accuracy = 0.01),
              flag = if_else(below_four_fifths, "Below 0.80", "")) |>
    kable(col.names = c(group_label, "Applicants", "Actual default rate", "Approval rate",
                        "Default rate among approved", "Impact ratio", "Four-fifths"),
          align = "lrrrrrl")
}

known_gender <- scored |> filter(gender != "XNA")
by_gender    <- group_outcomes(if_else(known_gender$gender == "F", "Female", "Male"),
                               known_gender$model_risk, known_gender$default, chosen_cutoff)
by_education <- group_outcomes(scored$education, scored$model_risk, scored$default, chosen_cutoff)
by_age       <- group_outcomes(scored$age_band, scored$model_risk, scored$default, chosen_cutoff)

n_xna <- sum(scored$gender == "XNA")
stopifnot(n_xna == 4,
          sum(by_gender$applicants) + n_xna == n_applicants,
          sum(by_education$applicants) == n_applicants,
          sum(by_age$applicants) == n_applicants)
```

```{r financial-compute}
# Financial impact at the chosen threshold. The benchmark (EXT_SOURCE_MEAN,
# as in business_impact.qmd) approves the same number of applicants.
model_path     <- approval_path(scored$model_risk, scored$default, scored$credit)
benchmark_path <- approval_path(-scored$ext_source, scored$default, scored$credit)

model_approved     <- scored$model_risk <= chosen_cutoff
n_approved         <- sum(model_approved)
benchmark_approved <- seq_len(n_applicants) %in% order(-scored$ext_source)[seq_len(n_approved)]
model_k     <- model_path[n_approved, ]
benchmark_k <- benchmark_path[n_approved, ]

stopifnot(model_k$defaults == sum(scored$default[model_approved]),
          benchmark_k$defaults == sum(scored$default[benchmark_approved]))

# Profit per 100,000 applicants for any approved set.
portfolio_profit <- function(approved, margin = base$margin, lgd = base$lgd) {
  (margin * sum(scored$credit[approved & !scored$default]) -
     lgd * sum(scored$credit[approved & scored$default])) * per_100k
}
model_profit <- portfolio_profit(model_approved)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(model_profit, base$profit)))

# BPS Q1 2019 figures, as in business_impact.qmd.
q1_impairment_eur  <- 430e6
annual_impairment  <- 4 * q1_impairment_eur
cost_of_risk       <- 0.0229   # quarterly: one quarter's impairment over loans
bps_loss_reduction <- 0.05     # BPS target: 5% fewer losses

financial <- list(
  vs_everyone      = model_profit - portfolio_profit(rep(TRUE, n_applicants)),
  vs_benchmark     = model_profit - portfolio_profit(benchmark_approved),
  defaults_avoided = (benchmark_k$defaults - model_k$defaults) * per_100k,
  count_reduction  = 1 - model_k$defaults / benchmark_k$defaults,
  credit_reduction = 1 - model_k$defaulted_credit / benchmark_k$defaulted_credit
)
financial$annual_saving <- annual_impairment * financial$credit_reduction
financial$bps_saving    <- annual_impairment * bps_loss_reduction

# business_impact.qmd's comparison: both scores at the benchmark's approval
# count under a 5% default-rate target.
bench_5 <- at_target_rate(benchmark_path, 0.05)
model_5 <- model_path[bench_5$approved, ]
financial$saving_at_5 <- annual_impairment * (1 - model_5$defaulted_credit / bench_5$defaulted_credit)
```

<!-- Phase 2 -->

# Executive summary

**Recommendation.** Use the model to support, not replace, approve/decline
decisions, declining applicants whose predicted probability of payment
difficulty is above **`r pct(chosen_cutoff, 0.1)`**. Before deployment, refit
the model with three changes to its inputs: remove family status; replace or
constrain the implied-term feature (`CREDIT_TERM`, payment divided by loan),
for example with the actual loan term or product type; and review the other
`r length(other_unclear)` inputs flagged as hard to explain in
[Adverse action mapping](#adverse-action-mapping). Adverse action notices must
state the principal reasons actually behind a decline, so an input that cannot
be explained to an applicant has to be fixed in the model, not filtered out
of the letter. Put the monitoring in
[Limitations and risks](#limitations-and-risks) in place at the same time.

**What the threshold means.** On training applicants scored by models that
had not seen them, the cutoff approves `r pct(at_chosen$metrics$approval_rate, 0.1)` of applicants and
cuts the default rate among those approved from
`r pct(mean(scored$default), 0.01)` to
`r pct(at_chosen$metrics$approved_default_rate, 0.01)`. It declines
`r pct(at_chosen$metrics$recall, 1)` of applicants who went on to default;
`r pct(1 - at_chosen$metrics$precision, 1)` of those declined would have
repaid, which is the trade that maximises profit at a 15% margin and 90% loss
given default. Any cutoff from `r pct(near_peak[1], 0.1)` to
`r pct(near_peak[2], 0.1)` earns within 0.1% of the maximum. If margins are
much thinner the cutoff should be stricter
(`r pct(optima$cutoff[optima$scenario == "Thin margin"], 0.1)` at a 5% margin).

**Expected financial impact.** Per 100,000 applicants, in the data's
currency, the cutoff earns `r money(financial$vs_everyone)` more than
approving everyone, and `r money(financial$vs_benchmark)` more than approving
the same number of applicants on the external credit scores alone, with
`r comma(financial$defaults_avoided)` fewer defaults. Against that benchmark
it holds `r pct(financial$credit_reduction, 0.1)` less defaulted credit.
Applied to Home Credit's annualised impairment losses
(EUR `r comma(annual_impairment / 1e6)`M), that is up to
EUR `r comma(financial$annual_saving / 1e6)`M a year. The business impact
analysis reported EUR `r comma(financial$saving_at_5 / 1e6)`M because it
compared the two scores at the 5% default-rate target, where both approve the
`r pct(bench_5$approval_rate, 0.1)` the benchmark approves; this card compares
them at the profit-optimal cutoff, where both approve
`r pct(n_approved / n_applicants, 0.1)`. Both figures are upper bounds,
because Home Credit's current process is stronger than the external scores
alone. The BPS target of a 5% loss reduction (EUR
`r comma(financial$bps_saving / 1e6)`M) needs
`r pct(bps_loss_reduction / financial$credit_reduction, 1)` of that edge.

**Key caveats.**

- **Training data.** The model learned only from applicants Home Credit
  approved, and its target is payment difficulty, not loss.
- **Fairness.** Approval rates for applicants aged `r flagged_age_range` fall
  below four-fifths of the oldest group's, in line with their higher actual
  default rates. Marital status is still a model input; removing it costs
  `r number(family_cost, accuracy = 0.0001)` AUC.
- **Explaining declines.** `r pct(mean(coverage$any_flagged), 1)` of declined
  applicants have a legally sensitive or hard-to-explain factor among their
  top three reasons, most often the implied term
  (`r pct(mean(coverage$any_term), 1)`). The implied term is also the
  feature that has drifted most between training and test applicants
  (standardised mean difference `r sprintf("%+.2f", term_smd)`). For
  `r pct(mean(coverage$first_opaque), 1)` the main reason is the opaque
  external credit scores.
- **Cost assumptions.** Margin and loss given default are external
  benchmarks, not Home Credit's own figures.

# Model details

```{r model-details}
booster    <- extract_fit_engine(final_fit)
n_features <- length(variable.names(booster))
n_raw_cols <- ncol(raw_train) - 2   # less SK_ID_CURR and TARGET
n_dropped  <- length(prepared$params$drop_cols)
```

- **Model:** gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost
  `r as.character(packageVersion("xgboost"))`, fitted through tidymodels).
  The output is a probability of payment difficulty (`TARGET` = 1), not an
  approve/decline verdict.
- **Version:** `xgb_tuned_final_nogender`, fitted on
  `r format(final$fitted_at, "%d %B %Y")`. This card was produced on
  `r format(Sys.Date(), "%d %B %Y")`.
- **Training data:** all `r comma(n_applicants)` applicants in
  `application_train` (Home Credit, via Kaggle, 2018), of whom
  `r pct(mean(scored$default), 0.01)` had payment difficulties. Only the
  application table is used. Of its `r n_raw_cols` input columns,
  `r n_dropped` mostly-empty ones are dropped. Engineered ratios, missing-value
  flags and one column per category level bring the model to
  `r n_features` features.
- **Tuning:** a 20-point random search on a 5,000-applicant sample, the best
  three re-scored on a 20% comparison sample, and the tree count chosen from
  500 to 2,000. No resampling for class imbalance: the modeling notebook
  compared down-sampling, up-sampling and SMOTE.

```{r hyperparameters}
param_labels <- c(
  trees          = "Number of trees",
  mtry           = "Features considered at each split",
  min_n          = "Minimum node size",
  tree_depth     = "Maximum tree depth",
  learn_rate     = "Learning rate",
  loss_reduction = "Minimum loss reduction to split",
  sample_size    = "Share of applicants sampled per tree"
)

tibble(parameter = names(param_labels),
       value = c(best_trees, map_dbl(names(param_labels)[-1], \(p) as.numeric(best_params[[p]])))) |>
  transmute(setting = param_labels[parameter],
            parameter = paste0("`", parameter, "`"),
            value = map_chr(value, \(v) format(signif(v, 5), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Setting", "Parameter", "Value"), align = "llr")
```

**Features excluded:**

- **`CODE_GENDER`**, for fairness: gender is a protected characteristic.
  Excluding it costs `r number(gender_cost, accuracy = 0.0001)` AUC.
- **The six supplementary tables** (credit bureau records, previous
  applications, payment histories) were not explored in the EDA and are not
  used.
- **Recommended before deployment: `NAME_FAMILY_STATUS`** (see
  [Fairness analysis](#fairness-analysis)).

# Intended use

**Intended use.** The model ranks Home Credit consumer-loan applicants by
their probability of payment difficulty. It supports approve/decline
decisions made by underwriters and policy, and lets management set a risk
appetite by moving the cutoff.

**Not intended for:**

- **Pricing** loans or setting interest rates.
- **Setting credit limits** or loan amounts.
- **Collections** or account management after a loan is made.
- **Applicants outside Home Credit's markets**, or populations unlike the
  training data.
- **Fully automated decisions without reason codes:** every decline needs
  reasons the applicant can be given (see
  [Adverse action mapping](#adverse-action-mapping)).

# Performance metrics

## Ranking accuracy (AUC)

```{r auc}
cv_auc  <- collect_metrics(cv_nogender$result) |> filter(.metric == "roc_auc")
oof_auc <- roc_auc_vec(scored$TARGET, scored$model_risk)

train_rows <- c(cv  = nrow(compare_data) * (CV_FOLDS - 1) / CV_FOLDS,
                oof = n_applicants * (CV_FOLDS - 1) / CV_FOLDS)

tibble(
  measure = c("Cross-validation, 20% comparison sample (3-fold)",
              "Out-of-fold, all training applicants (3-fold)",
              "Kaggle public leaderboard",
              "Kaggle private leaderboard"),
  rows_per_fit = c(comma(train_rows[["cv"]], accuracy = 1000),
                   comma(train_rows[["oof"]], accuracy = 1000),
                   comma(n_applicants), comma(n_applicants)),
  auc = c(number(cv_auc$mean, accuracy = 0.0001),
          number(oof_auc, accuracy = 0.0001),
          "0.75608", "0.75817")
) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Measure", "Training rows per fit", "AUC"), align = "lrr")
```

AUC is the chance that the model ranks a randomly chosen defaulter as riskier
than a randomly chosen repayer (0.5 is random, 1.0 perfect). The
out-of-fold and Kaggle scores
(`r number(oof_auc, accuracy = 0.001)` and 0.758) are above the
comparison-sample score (`r number(cv_auc$mean, accuracy = 0.001)`) because
each fit learns from more applicants: about
`r comma(train_rows[["oof"]], accuracy = 1000)` or all
`r comma(n_applicants)`, rather than
`r comma(train_rows[["cv"]], accuracy = 1000)`.

## Calibration

The threshold analysis below treats each predicted default probability as a
real probability. That only holds if the predictions are calibrated: among
applicants given a predicted risk of 10%, about 10% should default.

```{r calibration-folds}
scored |>
  group_by(fold) |>
  summarise(applicants        = n(),
            predicted_default = mean(model_risk),
            actual_default    = mean(default),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(fold = str_replace(fold, "Fold", "Fold "),
         applicants = comma(applicants),
         across(c(predicted_default, actual_default), \(x) pct(x, 0.01))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Fold", "Applicants", "Mean predicted default", "Actual default rate"),
        align = "lrrr")
```

```{r calibration}
#| fig-height: 4.5
calibration <- calibration_table(scored$model_risk, scored$default, n = 10)
stopifnot(sum(calibration$applicants) == n_applicants)

max_calibration_gap <- max(abs(calibration$predicted_default - calibration$actual_default))

ggplot(calibration, aes(predicted_default, actual_default)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey75", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = model_colour, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = model_colour, size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title    = "Predicted risk matches actual default rates",
       subtitle = "Out-of-fold predictions, applicants grouped into tenths by predicted risk",
       x = "Mean predicted default", y = "Actual default rate") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Across the ten risk groups, predicted and actual default rates differ by at
most `r number(max_calibration_gap * 100, accuracy = 0.01)` percentage points, and the mean prediction in
each fold is within
`r number(max(abs(tapply(scored$model_risk, scored$fold, mean) - tapply(scored$default, scored$fold, mean))) * 100, accuracy = 0.01)`
percentage points of the actual rate. Predicted probabilities can be read as
probabilities.

## At the chosen threshold

The model declines applicants whose predicted default probability is above
`r pct(chosen_cutoff, 0.1)` (chosen in the next section). Here a "positive"
is a predicted default, which means a decline.

```{r threshold-metrics}
m <- at_chosen$metrics

tibble(
  measure = c("Approval rate",
              "Default rate among approved applicants",
              "Precision: share of declined applicants who would have defaulted",
              "Recall: share of all defaulters the model declines"),
  value = pct(c(m$approval_rate, m$approved_default_rate, m$precision, m$recall))
) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Measure", "Value"), align = "lr")
```

Per 100,000 applicants:

```{r confusion}
at_chosen$confusion |>
  arrange(desc(outcome == "Would have defaulted")) |>
  mutate(Total = Approved + Declined,
         across(-outcome, \(x) comma(x, accuracy = 1))) |>
  select(outcome, Approved, Declined, Total) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Actual outcome", "Approved", "Declined", "Total"), align = "lrrr")
```

The overall default rate is `r pct(mean(scored$default), 0.01)`. Approving at
this threshold lowers that to `r pct(m$approved_default_rate, 0.01)` among
approved applicants, while declining
`r pct(1 - m$approval_rate, 0.1)` of applicants. Most declined applicants
(`r pct(1 - m$precision, 1)`) would have repaid: that is the price of catching
`r pct(m$recall, 1)` of defaulters, and the threshold analysis shows it is
the profit-maximising trade.

# Decision threshold analysis

## Break-even rule

Approving a loan of principal $C$ earns the margin $m \times C$ if it is
repaid and loses $\text{LGD} \times C$ if it defaults. With predicted default
probability $p$, the expected profit is

$$
(1 - p)\, m\, C \;-\; p \cdot \text{LGD} \cdot C,
$$

which is positive while

$$
p \;<\; \frac{m}{m + \text{LGD}}.
$$

Margin is net interest margin rather than net profit, because the threshold
decides the *marginal* loan, and most operating cost does not change with one
more approval. The thin-margin scenario covers the view that it does.

```{r assumptions}
tribble(
  ~input, ~base, ~sensitivity, ~source,
  "Margin on a repaid loan (share of principal)", "15%", "5%, 10%, 20%",
  "Home Credit B.V. FY2018 results: net interest margin 15.8% (homecredit.net, results announcement, 28 Jun 2019). BPS Q1 2019: net interest income EUR 889M on EUR 18,755M loans, about 19% annualised.",
  "Loss given default, LGD (share of principal)", "90%", "45%, 70%, 95%",
  "Typical unsecured consumer LGD about 90% (Vergent LMS, \"Loss Given Default\"); FTC (2013), \"The Structure and Practices of the Debt Buying Industry\": charged-off debt sold for about 4 cents per dollar (7.9 cents if under 3 years old). 45% is the Basel foundation-IRB LGD for senior unsecured claims (BIS CRE32), a lenient bound: TARGET marks payment difficulty, and some flagged loans recover.",
  "Recovery rate", "10%", "= 1 - LGD", "As above."
) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Input", "Base", "Sensitivity", "Source"))
```

```{r break-even}
scenarios |>
  transmute(scenario,
            margin     = pct(margin, 1),
            lgd        = pct(lgd, 1),
            break_even = pct(break_even, 0.1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Scenario", "Margin", "LGD", "Break-even predicted default"),
        align = "lrrr")
```

## Profit by cutoff

The rule above judges one loan at a time. To check it against actual
outcomes, every training applicant is approved if their out-of-fold predicted
default is at or below a cutoff, and the profit is totalled from what actually
happened:

$$
\text{profit} \;=\; m \sum_{\text{approved, repaid}} C \;-\; \text{LGD} \sum_{\text{approved, defaulted}} C,
$$

using each loan's raw `AMT_CREDIT` (in the data's currency, not converted),
for cutoffs from `r pct(min(cutoffs), 0.1)` to `r pct(max(cutoffs), 1)` in
steps of 0.5 points, per 100,000 applicants.

```{r profit-chart}
#| fig-height: 5.5
scenario_colours <- c("Base"             = model_colour,
                      "Lenient recovery" = "#2F9E44",
                      "Thin margin"      = "#E8590C",
                      "High margin"      = "#7048E8")

ggplot(scenario_curves, aes(cutoff, profit / 1e6, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = optima, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = optima, aes(label = pct(cutoff, 0.1)),
            vjust = -0.9, size = 3.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = scenario_colours) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), breaks = seq(0, 0.4, 0.05)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.1))) +
  labs(title    = "Profit peaks near each scenario's break-even cutoff",
       subtitle = "Profit per 100,000 applicants approving everyone at or below the cutoff",
       x = "Cutoff: highest predicted default approved",
       y = "Profit (millions, data currency)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left",
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r optima}
optima |>
  transmute(scenario,
            break_even        = pct(break_even, 0.1),
            optimal_cutoff    = pct(cutoff, 0.1),
            approval_rate     = pct(approval_rate, 0.1),
            approved_default  = pct(default_rate, 0.01),
            profit            = money(profit),
            vs_everyone       = paste0("+", money(vs_everyone))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Scenario", "Break-even", "Optimal cutoff", "Approval rate",
                      "Default rate among approved", "Profit per 100k",
                      "vs approve everyone"),
        align = "lrrrrrr")
```

In every scenario the empirical optimum lands within
`r number(max(abs(optima$cutoff - optima$break_even)) * 100, accuracy = 0.1)`
points of the break-even rule, as calibrated predictions should. The
base-case curve is flat near its peak: every cutoff from
`r pct(near_peak[1], 0.1)` to `r pct(near_peak[2], 0.1)` earns within 0.1% of
the maximum, so the exact cutoff matters less than being in that range.

## Sensitivity

The optimal cutoff for each combination of margin and LGD:

```{r sensitivity}
#| fig-height: 4
sensitivity <- expand_grid(margin = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20),
                           lgd    = c(0.45, 0.70, 0.90, 0.95)) |>
  mutate(optimal = map2_dbl(margin, lgd, \(m, l) {
           p <- add_profit(sweep, m, l)
           p$cutoff[which.max(p$profit)]
         }),
         break_even = break_even_cutoff(margin, lgd))

stopifnot(all(sensitivity$optimal > min(cutoffs) & sensitivity$optimal < max(cutoffs)))

ggplot(sensitivity, aes(factor(lgd), factor(margin), fill = optimal)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%s\n(break-even %s)", pct(optimal, 0.1), pct(break_even, 0.1)),
                colour = optimal > 0.2),
            size = 3.3, lineheight = 0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#EDF2FF", high = "#364FC7", guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey15", `TRUE` = "white")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) percent(as.numeric(x))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) percent(as.numeric(x))) +
  labs(title    = "Thinner margins and higher losses call for a stricter cutoff",
       subtitle = "Optimal cutoff (break-even rule in brackets)",
       x = "Loss given default", y = "Margin") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

## Comparison with the 5% risk-appetite cutoff

```{r target-compare}
cutoff_5   <- sort(scored$model_risk)[at_target_rate(model_path, 0.05)$approved]

at_5 <- add_profit(cutoff_sweep(scored$model_risk, scored$default, scored$credit, cutoff_5),
                   base$margin, base$lgd)
at_chosen_profit <- add_profit(cutoff_sweep(scored$model_risk, scored$default, scored$credit,
                                            chosen_cutoff),
                               base$margin, base$lgd)

tibble(rule = c("Profit-maximising (base case, chosen)", "5% default-rate target"),
       cutoff = c(chosen_cutoff, cutoff_5),
       approval_rate = c(at_chosen_profit$approval_rate, at_5$approval_rate),
       default_rate  = c(at_chosen_profit$default_rate, at_5$default_rate),
       profit        = c(at_chosen_profit$profit, at_5$profit)) |>
  mutate(cutoff = pct(cutoff, 0.1), approval_rate = pct(approval_rate, 0.1),
         default_rate = pct(default_rate, 0.01), profit = money(profit)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Rule", "Cutoff", "Approval rate", "Default rate among approved",
                      "Profit per 100k"),
        align = "lrrrr")
```

The business impact analysis set the cutoff from a risk appetite: approve
as many applicants as possible while keeping the default rate among them at
5%, which gave a cutoff of `r pct(cutoff_5, 0.1)`. The profit-maximising
cutoff under the base case is `r pct(chosen_cutoff, 0.1)`, within
`r number(abs(chosen_cutoff - cutoff_5) * 100, accuracy = 0.1)` points, and the
5% target earns `r money(at_chosen_profit$profit - at_5$profit)` less per
100,000 applicants
(`r pct((at_chosen_profit$profit - at_5$profit) / at_chosen_profit$profit, 0.01)`).
The two ways of setting the threshold agree.

**Chosen threshold: decline applicants with a predicted default probability
above `r pct(chosen_cutoff, 0.1)`.** It is the base-case optimum, rounded to
the nearest 0.5 points, and it is used for every result in the rest of this
card.

**Caveat.** Margin and LGD are applied to the full principal over the loan's
life. That ignores timing (interest is earned over months, losses arrive
later), partial repayment before default, and discounting.

# Explainability

## Method

The model's decisions are explained with **SHAP values**, computed with
XGBoost's built-in TreeSHAP. For each applicant, SHAP splits the predicted
log-odds of default into one contribution per feature, measured against the
model's baseline for an average applicant. The contributions add up exactly
to the applicant's prediction.

The explanations use a random sample of 1,000 applicants from the **test
set**: applicants the model never saw during training, as a new applicant
would be. Their outcomes are unknown, so this section explains decisions but
does not judge whether they were right. The final model's predictions on the
test set are spread like the out-of-fold predictions the threshold was set
on, so the chosen cutoff applies to them:

```{r shap-sample}
test_risk   <- predict(final_fit, test, type = "prob")$.pred_1

probs <- c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90)
rbind(`Out-of-fold (training applicants)`   = quantile(scored$model_risk, probs),
      `Final model (all test applicants)`   = quantile(test_risk, probs),
      `Final model (1,000-applicant sample)` = quantile(shap_risk, probs)) |>
  apply(2, \(x) pct(x, 0.1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Predicted default at percentiles of each distribution", align = "rrrrr")
```

## Most influential factors

Features that encode the same thing about the applicant are combined: age
appears as birth date, age in years and age band; the external scores as
each score plus their mean, minimum, maximum and count; a category as one
column per level. Each bar below is one thing about the applicant.

```{r importance-chart}
#| fig-height: 6
importance |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_abs, fct_reorder(factor, mean_abs))) +
  geom_col(fill = model_colour, width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title    = "External credit scores dominate the model's decisions",
       subtitle = "Mean absolute SHAP value (log-odds), 1,000 test applicants, top 15 factors",
       x = "Mean |SHAP| (log-odds of default)", y = NULL) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot",
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

External credit scores account for
`r pct(importance$share[importance$factor == "External credit scores"], 1)` of
the total, more than the next
`r sum(cumsum(importance$share[-1]) <= importance$share[1])` factors combined.

The ten most influential individual features, one dot per applicant. Dots to
the right raise predicted risk; colour shows the applicant's value of that
feature, from low to high:

```{r beeswarm}
#| fig-height: 6
shap_matrix  <- as.matrix(select(shap_wide, -.row))
shown_values <- feature_values

# Shorter display names for long dummy columns.
short_name <- \(x) str_replace(x, "^NAME_EDUCATION_TYPE_(.*)$", "EDUCATION = \\1")
colnames(shap_matrix) <- short_name(colnames(shap_matrix))
names(shown_values)   <- short_name(names(shown_values))

sv <- shapviz(shap_matrix, X = shown_values, baseline = baseline_log_odds)

sv_importance(sv, kind = "beeswarm", max_display = 10, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) +
  labs(title    = "How each feature's value moves predicted risk",
       subtitle = "SHAP value per applicant, 1,000 test applicants",
       x = "SHAP value (log-odds of default)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

```{r direction-table}
importance |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  left_join(factor_map, by = "factor") |>
  transmute(rank = row_number(), factor, share = pct(share, 0.1), direction) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Rank", "Factor", "Share of total |SHAP|", "Direction"),
        align = "rlrl")
```

```{r age-effect}
age_effect <- grouped |>
  filter(factor == "Age") |>
  mutate(age_band = shap_sample$AGE_BAND[.row]) |>
  group_by(age_band) |>
  summarise(applicants = n(), mean_contribution = mean(contribution), .groups = "drop")

older_effect <- age_effect |>
  filter(as.numeric(str_extract(age_band, "\\d+")) >= 60)
```

Age's contribution is not monotone. Once the other factors are known,
applicants in their 30s and 40s get the largest increase from age, while the
youngest and oldest get a decrease:

```{r age-table}
age_effect |>
  mutate(mean_contribution = number(mean_contribution, accuracy = 0.001)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Age band", "Applicants in sample", "Mean age contribution (log-odds)"),
        align = "lrr")
```

# Adverse action mapping

A declined applicant is entitled to the main reasons for the decision. Each
factor below maps the condition that raises an applicant's risk to the reason
text a decline letter would use. The table covers the ten most influential
factors and every factor that is among the top three reasons for any of the
sampled applicants the model would decline. Flags mark factors that are
legally sensitive, hard to explain to an applicant, or opaque third-party
scores.

```{r adverse-map}
importance |>
  filter(factor %in% union(top_factors$factor, declined_top3$factor)) |>
  left_join(factor_map, by = "factor") |>
  left_join(declined_counts, by = "factor") |>
  transmute(factor, condition, reason,
            in_top3 = replace_na(in_top3, 0L),
            flag = if_else(flag == "", type, paste0(type, ": ", flag))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Factor", "Raises risk when", "Reason given to applicant",
                      sprintf("Top-3 reason for (of %d declined)", length(declined_rows)),
                      "Flag"),
        align = "lllrl")
```

- **External credit scores** are third-party scores whose inputs Home Credit
  does not see, so the reason can only be generic.
- **Age** may be used in an empirically derived system under ECOA, but not to
  the detriment of elderly applicants. In this sample, the mean age
  contribution for applicants 60 and over is
  `r number(weighted.mean(older_effect$mean_contribution, older_effect$applicants), accuracy = 0.001)`
  log-odds (`r if_else(weighted.mean(older_effect$mean_contribution, older_effect$applicants) < 0, "it lowers their predicted risk", "it raises their predicted risk")`).
- **Education level** and **family status** are proxy and protected-basis
  concerns: marital status is a prohibited basis under ECOA, and both remain
  in the model.

## Examples

Three test applicants above the `r pct(chosen_cutoff, 0.1)` cutoff, the
applicants at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentile of predicted risk among
those the model would decline:

```{r adverse-examples}
#| results: asis
picks <- map_int(c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75), \(q) {
  target <- quantile(shap_risk[declined_rows], q, type = 1)
  declined_rows[which.min(abs(shap_risk[declined_rows] - target))]
})
stopifnot(length(unique(picks)) == 3, all(shap_risk[picks] > chosen_cutoff))

examples <- grouped |>
  filter(.row %in% picks, contribution > 0) |>
  group_by(.row) |>
  slice_max(contribution, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(factor_map, by = "factor")
stopifnot(!anyNA(examples$reason))

for (i in seq_along(picks)) {
  r <- picks[i]
  cat(sprintf("\n**Applicant %s** (test ID %s): predicted default %s\n\n",
              LETTERS[i], shap_sample$SK_ID_CURR[r], pct(shap_risk[r], 0.1)))
  examples |>
    filter(.row == r) |>
    arrange(desc(contribution)) |>
    transmute(rank = row_number(), factor, reason,
              log_odds = number(contribution, accuracy = 0.01),
              type) |>
    kable(col.names = c("Rank", "Factor", "Reason given", "Contribution (log-odds)", "Flag"),
          align = "rllrl") |>
    print()
  cat("\n")
}
```

`r length(declined_rows)` of the 1,000 sampled applicants
(`r pct(length(declined_rows) / 1000, 0.1)`) would be declined at the chosen
cutoff. Of these:

- `r pct(mean(coverage$any_flagged), 1)` have at least one legally sensitive
  or hard-to-explain factor among their top three reasons. The implied-term
  factor alone appears for `r pct(mean(coverage$any_term), 1)`.
- `r pct(mean(coverage$any_sensitive), 1)` have a legally sensitive factor in
  their top three.
- For `r pct(mean(coverage$first_flagged), 1)` the main reason is flagged.
  For `r pct(mean(coverage$first_opaque), 1)` it is the external credit
  scores, which can only be explained generically.

Adverse action notices must state the principal reasons actually behind a
decline, so flagged factors cannot be skipped or reworded at the letter
stage. The fix belongs in the model: before deployment, replace or constrain
the implied-term feature (for example with the actual loan term or product
type) and review the other inputs flagged as hard to explain.

# Fairness analysis

`CODE_GENDER` is excluded from the model, which costs
`r number(gender_cost, accuracy = 0.0001)` AUC on the comparison folds.
Excluding a protected attribute does not by itself make outcomes fair: age and education remain in the model and the EDA
found both correlate with protected characteristics. This section checks
outcomes at the `r pct(chosen_cutoff, 0.1)` cutoff on out-of-fold
predictions.

The **adverse impact ratio** is a group's approval rate divided by the
highest group's. Under the four-fifths rule, a ratio below 0.80 is evidence
of adverse impact worth reviewing. The rule comes from US employment
guidance (the EEOC's Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures);
here it is a screening heuristic, not a legal test for lending. The actual
default rate is shown next to it: a gap in approval that follows a gap in repayment is the model doing its
job; a gap that does not is a problem.

## Gender

```{r fairness-gender}
fairness_table(by_gender, "Gender")
```

`r n_xna` applicants with gender recorded as `XNA` (unknown) are left out.

## Education

```{r fairness-education}
fairness_table(by_education |> arrange(desc(applicants)), "Education")
```

## Age

```{r fairness-age}
fairness_table(by_age, "Age band")
```

## Family status

`NAME_FAMILY_STATUS` (marital status) is still in the model, and marital
status is a prohibited basis under ECOA. Excluding it as well, with
everything else in the final configuration unchanged, changes AUC on the
comparison folds by:

```{r family-cost}
family_paired |>
  transmute(fold = str_replace(id, "Fold", "Fold "),
            with_family    = number(xgb_tuned_nogender, accuracy = 0.0001),
            without_family = number(xgb_tuned_nogender_nofamily, accuracy = 0.0001),
            cost           = number(difference, accuracy = 0.0001)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Fold", "AUC with family status", "AUC without", "Cost of excluding"),
        align = "lrrr")
```

The mean cost is `r number(family_cost, accuracy = 0.0001)` AUC
(`r sum(family_paired$difference > 0)` of 3 folds lower without it), against
`r number(gender_cost, accuracy = 0.0001)` for `CODE_GENDER`.

**Recommendation before deployment:** refit the final model without
`NAME_FAMILY_STATUS`. The measured cost is small, and keeping a prohibited
basis as a model input is a legal risk that the accuracy does not justify.
This card describes the model as fitted, with family status included; the
refit would need its own out-of-fold check before replacing it.

# Limitations and risks

```{r limitations-compute}
ext1_missing <- mean(is.na(raw_train$EXT_SOURCE_1))
no_ext_score <- sum(train$EXT_SOURCE_COUNT == 0)
ext_share    <- importance$share[importance$factor == "External credit scores"]

bureau_col   <- "AMT_REQ_CREDIT_BUREAU_QRT"
bureau_na    <- is.na(raw_train[[bureau_col]])
bureau_fill  <- prepared$params$numeric_medians[[bureau_col]]
bureau_zero  <- !bureau_na & raw_train[[bureau_col]] == 0
# All six enquiry counts are missing on the same rows.
stopifnot(bureau_fill == 0,
          all(map_lgl(select(raw_train, starts_with("AMT_REQ_CREDIT_BUREAU")),
                      \(x) identical(is.na(x), bureau_na))))
```

- **Approved applicants only.** The training data holds only applicants Home
  Credit approved. How declined applicants would have repaid is unknown (no
  reject inference), so the model may misjudge applicant types the current
  process screens out.
- **`TARGET` marks payment difficulty, not loss.** Some flagged loans recover
  in full. The profit figures treat every default as a loss of
  `r pct(base$lgd, 1)` of principal.
- **Application table only.** Credit bureau history, previous applications
  and payment histories are not used. They may hold signal the model misses.
- **Data context.** One lender's applicants, circa 2018. Amounts are in the
  data's own currency, not converted, so financial figures per 100,000
  applicants are in that currency. Only the BPS scaling is in euros.
- **Drift between training and test applicants.** Test loans are smaller
  relative to income and carry shorter implied terms. A standardised mean
  difference above 0.1 is worth a closer look:

```{r drift-table}
drift |>
  transmute(feature = paste0("`", predictor, "`"),
            across(c(train_median, test_median), \(x)
              map_chr(x, \(v) format(signif(v, 3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))),
            flag = if_else(abs(smd) > 0.1, "Above 0.1", ""),
            smd  = number(smd, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  relocate(flag, .after = last_col()) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Feature", "Train median", "Test median", "Standardised mean difference", ""),
        align = "lrrrl")
```

- **Heavy reliance on external scores.** External credit scores carry
  `r pct(ext_share, 1)` of the model's SHAP importance, but their inputs are
  unknown to Home Credit. `EXT_SOURCE_1` is missing for
  `r pct(ext1_missing, 1)` of applicants, and `r comma(no_ext_score)` have
  no external score at all.
- **Proxies for protected traits.** Gender is excluded, but age, education,
  marital status, region and social-circle defaults remain inputs. Approval
  rates for applicants aged `r flagged_age_range` fall below the four-fifths
  line.
- **Bureau enquiries: missing counted as zero.** `r pct(mean(bureau_na), 1)`
  of applicants have no bureau-enquiry record (`r bureau_col` and the other
  enquiry counts are missing). Data preparation filled these with the
  median, `r bureau_fill`, so "no enquiries" mixes in "no bureau record".
  The two groups default at different rates
  (`r pct(mean(raw_train$TARGET[bureau_na]), 0.1)` with no record,
  `r pct(mean(raw_train$TARGET[bureau_zero]), 0.1)` with zero recorded
  enquiries). This is a data-preparation issue to fix in a refit, for example
  with a missing-value flag.
- **Legal reference.** The legal flags in this card use the US Equal Credit
  Opportunity Act (ECOA) as the reference. Home Credit's markets have their
  own consumer-lending and anti-discrimination rules, which a deployment
  review would need to apply.
- **Cost assumptions are external benchmarks.** The 15% margin and 90% loss
  given default come from published figures and industry norms, not Home
  Credit's own loan-level economics. The chosen cutoff moves with them (see
  [Sensitivity](#sensitivity)).

## Monitoring

Once deployed, the model should be checked regularly against these triggers:

- **Input drift:** standardised mean difference of the key features between
  recent applicants and the training data. Review above 0.1.
- **Calibration:** predicted against actual default rate by tenth of
  predicted risk, as outcomes mature. The threshold math depends on it.
- **Approval rates by group:** gender, education and age band, with impact
  ratios. Review any group below 0.80, or any change since deployment.
- **Decline reasons:** how often each reason, and each flagged factor, is
  cited.
- **Ranking:** AUC on matured loans against the
  `r number(oof_auc, accuracy = 0.001)` out-of-fold baseline.

# Use of AI

I used Claude in two ways. In chat, it researched the cost assumptions and
their sources, wrote the brief for this card, and reviewed each stage of the
output. In Claude Code, it wrote the R code and drafted the text. I reviewed
and approved each analytic decision, including scoring SHAP on unseen test
applicants and measuring the cost of excluding family status, and I rewrote
the narrative in my own words.
